IB Computer Science

B1.1 Problem Specification

Topic B1: Computational Thinking | Define the Problem Before Code

Retrieval Practice

Interleave recall from B3 (OOP) before we shift to problem-solving.

  1. What is encapsulation?
  2. What does polymorphism allow us to do?
  3. Which design pattern fits “notify many subscribers when state changes”?

Press Down for answers

Answer 1

What is encapsulation?

Bundling data with methods and restricting direct access to internal state.

Answer 2

What does polymorphism allow us to do?

Treat different types through a shared interface/superclass so one piece of code works for many types.

Answer 3

Which design pattern fits “notify many subscribers when state changes”?

Observer

The Big Question

🤔 Why do many software projects fail… even with good programmers?

The code works — but the system still doesn’t meet the real need.

❌ Misconception: “Programming is the hard part; requirements are obvious.”

Ambiguity and conflicting needs are common — and expensive if discovered late.

✅ Key idea: a clear problem specification is the foundation.

In IB, this thinking feeds directly into IA Criterion A (planning and success criteria).

Stakeholders

Who gets affected when a system changes — and who gets to decide?

Users, owners, clients, developers, administrators, regulators…

Stakeholders often have conflicting priorities (cost vs features vs security).

Example

A school timetable system: students, teachers, administrators, parents.

🧠 Quick Check

For an online shop, name two stakeholders other than the developer.

Examples: customers, store owner, payment provider, delivery partners, support staff.

What goes into a Problem Specification?

What must be true before we can claim “the solution works”?

Problem statement: what needs solving (and why)?

Objectives: what outcomes do stakeholders want?

Constraints/limitations: what restricts the solution?

Input/Output: what data comes in and what results go out?

Evaluation criteria: how we will measure success.

Inputs & Outputs (System Boundary)

How does information enter the system, and what must the system produce?

Inputs

Manual: keyboard, touchscreen, mouse

Automatic: sensors (temperature, light, pressure)

Direct data entry: barcode, OCR, OMR, MICR

Outputs

Temporary: screen display

Permanent: printout

Physical: actuators (relays, motors)

Trade-off: manual input is cheaper but error-prone; automatic input can be faster and more accurate but costly.

Constraints & Limitations

What might prevent a “perfect” solution in the real world?

Regional differences: languages, currencies, time zones, units.

Legal: data protection (e.g., GDPR), consumer laws.

Cultural: colour meanings, accessibility, RTL vs LTR layouts.

🧠 Quick Check

Give one legal constraint a social media app must consider in Europe.

Example: GDPR requirements for consent, data minimisation, and user rights (access/erasure).

Evaluation Criteria

How do we avoid “It seems good” as our definition of success?

Criteria should be specific and measurable.

They link directly to stakeholder needs.

Examples

“Search returns results in under 1 second for 10,000 items.”

“System supports 3 languages and correct date formats.”

“Users can reset passwords within 2 minutes.”

🧠 Quick Check

Which is better: “The UI is good” or “Users can complete checkout in under 2 minutes”?

The measurable one — “complete checkout in under 2 minutes”.

Misconception Check

A. Stakeholders are only the people who use the system directly.

B. Constraints and limitations shape what solutions are feasible.

C. Evaluation criteria should be vague so they’re “easy to meet”.

D. Input/output specifications clarify the system boundary.

Press Down for answers

Answers

A: False. Owners, regulators, support teams, and others are stakeholders too.

B: True. They constrain what the system can do and how it must behave.

C: False. Criteria should be specific and measurable to be meaningful.

D: True. They define how data enters/leaves the system.

Key Takeaways

  • A clear problem specification prevents wasted effort and misaligned solutions.
  • Identify stakeholders and translate needs into requirements.
  • Define inputs/outputs, constraints, and measurable evaluation criteria.
